Tier A diagnostic · WHO / UN life expectancy 2000–2015

This dataset can rank countries. It cannot rank the levers a funder would pull.

A digit-level corruption in ten of nineteen numeric columns, a merge failure that deletes twenty-five countries’ economics, and a panel structure that inflates every naive validation — and what survives all three.

SituationThe WHO/UN life-expectancy panel — 183 countries, 2,928 country-years, 2000–2015 — is the default free evidence base for “what drives life expectancy”. Its standard output is a driver ranking in which schooling, income and health spending dominate.
ComplicationThat ranking does not survive three checks the standard workflow never runs. The character 0 has been deleted from every value in ten columns including the outcome; a quarter of the economic data is missing because of a country-name join failure that preferentially deletes rich countries; and the driver coefficients are estimated across countries that differ in a thousand unmeasured ways, then reported as if they were levers.
ResolutionAfter repair and with country fixed effects, ten of twelve predictors lose their effect entirely. Two survive — disease burden and schooling — and the predictive model is beaten by copying last year’s number.
Once you stop comparing rich countries to poor ones, only two of twelve factors still move with a country’s own life expectancy — HIV/AIDS burden (-1.58 years per SD) and schooling (+0.95 years per SD); everything else this dataset is famous for, including GDP and health spending, is a description of development rather than a lever on it.
  1. The instrument is broken in three separate ways. Ten columns contain no 0 digit at all — GDP has none in 2,490 values where 57% of them should — damaging an estimated 6,217 cells including roughly one life-expectancy value in ten. Twenty-five countries have no GDP for any of the sixteen years because their WHO name never matched a World Bank key. And Status labels France, Canada and Finland “Developing”.
  2. The famous drivers are country traits, not levers. Pooled R² 0.889 collapses to a within-country 0.488 — country and year fixed effects absorb 45% of the apparent explanatory power. Log GDP shrinks 97%, health-spend share 94%, adult mortality 89%. Only 2 of 12 predictors survive.
  3. The predictive claim needs two corrections. Splitting by row instead of by country overstates accuracy by 0.042 R² and understates error 2.1×. On a temporal holdout the 28-feature model scores MAE 1.05 years and carrying last year’s value forward scores 0.88 — the model is 19% worse than doing nothing.

Recommendation

The analytics lead should (1) stop using this file to prioritise between education, income and health-spending investments, and reclassify existing driver claims built on it as descriptive rankings; (2) add the digit-integrity audit and the all-periods-missing check to the ingestion template — both are ten lines and both fired here; (3) require every panel study to report a within-country specification and every forecast to beat carry-forward as a review gate; and (4) use the model only as a surveillance gap-filler for countries with no reported value, at a measured 1.54-year error against a 6.30-year baseline.

Context · The one unambiguous fact

Life expectancy rose 4.9 years globally and the development gap narrowed by 1.6

Before the criticism, the agreement: every group improved. The global mean moved from 66.5 to 71.4 years between 2000 and 2015, and the gap between developed and developing countries closed from 13.1 to 11.5 years. This is the finding the dataset supports without qualification — and it is descriptive, not a lever.

So what
A trend this smooth also sets the bar for Part III: if life expectancy moves ~0.3 years a year, last year’s value is a very strong predictor of this year’s — which is why no model here is scored without comparing it to persistence.

Part I · The instrument

Ten columns contain no digit “0” at all, and one of them is the outcome

In any naturally occurring numeric column the digits after the leading one are close to uniform, so roughly one value in ten should contain a 0. Ten columns contain none. The probability under that null is below 1e-100 for every one of them.

So what
This is not a data-quality quibble but a deterministic string bug that damaged an estimated 6,217 cells. It passes every null check, dtype check and range check, which is why it has survived in one of the most-downloaded datasets on Kaggle. The audit that finds it is ten lines of code.

The corruption is reversible where the panel is informative. Italy 2004 reads a world-record 89.0 years; its digits are 809, and restoring the deleted zero gives 80.9 — which sits exactly between the 79.9 before it and the 81.2 after. Barbados’ adult mortality reads …111, 19, 16, 14, 12, 11, 1, 98 and reconstructs to a smooth …111, 109, 106, 104, 102, 101, 100, 98.

1,128 cells were repaired, each with a ledger row recording the delivered value, the reconstructed value and the robust panel fit that justified it. Recovery is partial and reported as such:

Where the repair fails. GDP and Population are estimated at 57% and 44% corrupted — beyond the ~29% contamination a robust fit tolerates, so the anchor itself is mostly damaged. They are left exactly as delivered, marked untrustworthy, and never given an interpreted coefficient. There is no way to recover them from inside the file.

Twenty-five countries have no GDP because their name never matched

So what
The missingness is total per country — sixteen of sixteen years — which is the signature of a failed join key, not of a country that reports irregularly. The affected names are United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, United States of America, Republic of Korea, Czechia, Viet Nam. This is MNAR and not imputable from inside the file.

The corruption is visible in ordinary exploratory analysis

So what
As delivered, the third adult-mortality decile shows 14 years more life expectancy than the second. The natural conclusion — “adult mortality is noisy here” — is wrong; the column was damaged. Repair cuts the wrong-way jump to 6 years and moves Spearman from -0.65 to -0.85. Corruption does not merely add noise, it destroys the shape of a relationship.

Part II · The signal

Most of what looks like a driver is a difference between countries

So what
For schooling, income composition and log GDP the overwhelming majority of variance is between countries. Only the remainder is movement a country actually experienced — and only that remainder can inform “what happens if we change this”.
So what
Pooled R² 0.889 becomes a within-country 0.488. Ten of twelve predictors lose their effect almost entirely: log GDP by 97%, health-spend share by 94%, adult mortality by 89%, and all three immunisation columns by 83–87%. The standard driver ranking is a ranking of countries by development, re-described as a menu of interventions.

Two factors survive, and one of them is actionable

So what
HIV/AIDS at -1.58 years per SD [-2.08, -1.08] and schooling at 0.95 [0.43, 1.47] — in raw units, 0.34 years of life expectancy per additional year of schooling. Every other confidence interval crosses zero.

This is what keeps the finding from being nihilism. The same protocol that refuses to credit GDP, health spending and immunisation coverage identifies these two decisively — so the null results are a calibrated statement about what the data can detect, not a failure of method.

The brief’s own policy question, answered

“For developing countries, does an increase in schooling or income composition associate with life-expectancy gains more than health expenditure?” Within-country and net of year effects, across 1,813 country-years:

leveryears per SD 95% CIverdict
Schooling1.30 [0.32, 2.29] distinguishable from zero
Health-spend share0.11 [-0.07, 0.29] not distinguishable

Schooling is the only one of the four candidate levers this dataset can distinguish from zero; health expenditure is not. The ranking is stable across all three cleaning variants. The honest caveat: a country’s schooling moved by a median of only ~0.55 years over the whole sixteen, so the realistic in-sample effect is well under a year of life expectancy.

The strongest predictor in the file partly is the outcome

Income composition of resources tops every correlation table at ρ = 0.91. It is documented as an income index, but within a country it correlates 0.86 with schooling and only 0.26 with log GDP — the opposite of what an income index would do. Adding life expectancy to a regression of this column on GDP and schooling lifts R² from 0.875 to 0.937. It behaves like a composite development index that partly embeds the target, so it is excluded from every driver specification.

A predictor that beats every other predictor deserves an audit, not a promotion. This check belongs in the ingestion template next to the digit audit.

Part III · The limits

Splitting by row instead of by country makes the model look 2.1× more accurate than it is

So what
Rows for the same country are near-duplicates: the between-country SD of mean life expectancy is 9.1 years, the median within-country SD across sixteen years is 1.5. A random split hands the model 2014 Afghanistan and grades it on 2015 Afghanistan. Any accuracy claim from this dataset that does not name its split rule should be discounted.

A 24-feature model loses to copying last year’s number

So what
Life expectancy is a slow-moving stock with enormous persistence, so a covariate model must beat persistence to justify itself — and this one does not. The covariates are informative about the level of life expectancy in a country never seen before and uninformative about change in a country already observed. Those are different products, and only the first is deliverable.

Dropping rows with any missing value deletes 50 of 183 countries

So what
Complete-case analysis keeps 54.5% of rows and deletes 50 countries outright — Japan, Denmark, Finland, Iceland, the United Kingdom and the United States among them. The deletion is not random: it is driven by the name-join failure, so it systematically removes high-income countries. Every complete-case regression on this dataset is fitted to a sample poorer than the world it claims to describe.

Where the model does earn its place

For a country with no reported life expectancy, the model predicts to 1.54 years against 6.30 for the only alternative available — a development-group mean. That is the one deployable product, and it ships with its regional error table attached rather than a single global figure:

Appendix · Methodology & limitations

What this analysis does not claim

No coefficient here is causal. Country fixed effects remove time-invariant confounders only. They do not remove time-varying confounding, they do not resolve reverse causation (life expectancy raises schooling as readily as the reverse), and they amplify attenuation from the measurement error documented in Part I. Path C is out of scope for this dataset: there is no treatment date, no assignment mechanism, no instrument and no untreated donor pool. The HIV/AIDS result in particular coincides with antiretroviral rollout and donor financing that this file does not measure.

Data and lineage

WHO Global Health Observatory + UN economic data, merged and published on Kaggle (2018). 2,928 country-years across 183 countries, 2000–2015. The delivered file contains 2,938 rows: ten “countries” appear once (2013 only) and all ten have a null life expectancy, so they are removed — the panel is 183×16, not the 193×16 the documentation describes.

Cleaning decisions

  • Digit repair — 1,128 cells across 9 fixed-precision columns, every one ledgered. GDP and Population deliberately not repaired.
  • Zero-coded missing — percentage expenditure (611 rows), Income composition (130), Schooling (28) converted to null. These are invisible to isnull() and materially change the panel estimates.
  • Mislabelled status — France, Canada, Israel, Greece, Finland and Republic of Korea are labelled “Developing”. Both the original and a corrected column ship.
  • Renamed misleading columns — BMI (range 1.0–87.3, not a BMI) → bmi_index; percentage expenditure (a per-capita USD level, not a percentage) → health_spend_per_capita_usd; Measles (raw case counts) → measles_cases.
  • Outliers retained with reasons — Haiti 2010 (36.3 years) is the earthquake and is real; the repair correctly leaves it alone.

Statistical methods

Mann-Whitney and Kruskal-Wallis for the non-normal outcome; Spearman with Fisher-z intervals; Benjamini-Hochberg FDR across the regional contrasts and correlations; effect sizes (Cohen’s d with bootstrap CIs, ε²) reported alongside every p-value. Panel estimates are two-way (country + year) fixed effects with country-clustered standard errors, justified by residual autocorrelation of r = 0.75. Predictive validation is GroupKFold by country plus a temporal holdout; all imputation and scaling is fitted inside the fold.

Sensitivity

Every headline result was recomputed on three dataset variants — as delivered, repaired, and with the suspect cells nulled. The verdicts are unchanged: HIV/AIDS and schooling survive fixed effects on all three, the economic and immunisation blocks fail on all three, and the carry-forward baseline beats the model on all three.

Fairness and governance

Country-level public aggregates; no personal data, so a person-level fairness audit is not applicable and is recorded as such rather than skipped. The representation audit does apply and was executed: complete-case analysis removes 50 countries and lowers the Developed share of the sample from 20.8% to 18.7%. Model error is reported per WHO region because a global MAE hides that accuracy is worst where covariate data is thinnest — which is exactly where a funder would want to use it.

Deployment ceiling

The data ends in 2015; nothing here is validated for use in 2026. The model card lists the gap-filler’s intended use and its four out-of-scope uses, including forecasting and lever ranking.

Reproducibility

Six numbered notebooks run in order from the raw CSV with no local module imports; RANDOM_STATE = 42 throughout; dependencies pinned in requirements.txt. Every number in this report is read from reports/_key_figures.json and the CSVs written by notebooks 03–05 — none is typed by hand.

WHO Global Health Observatory + UN · 2000–2015 · 2,928 country-years, 183 countries.
Tier A analysis to the McKinsey communication standard — answer-first, MECE, action titles, a “So what” under every exhibit. Generated 2026-07-31.
